02.01.title: Vectors and geometry
02.01.html:
A force has a size and a direction, and so does a velocity, a displacement or a moment. Vectors are the bookkeeping that keeps both together. Two products do most of the work in mechanics: the dot product measures how much one vector points along another, and the cross product builds the moment of a force about a point.

Components and length

In a Cartesian frame a vector is a list of components, a=(a1​,a2​,a3​). Its length follows from Pythagoras:

∣a∣=a12​+a22​+a32​​.

Adding vectors adds components, and scaling multiplies each one. That is the whole algebra; the geometry comes from the two products.

The dot product

a⋅b=a1​b1​+a2​b2​+a3​b3​=∣a∣∣b∣cosθ.

The second form gives the angle between two vectors, and it says a⋅b=0 exactly when they’re perpendicular. Dividing by ∣a∣ gives the scalar projection of b on a, the length of the shadow b casts on the line of a. The vector projection is

proja​b=a⋅aa⋅b​a.

Mechanical work is a dot product: W=F⋅s. Only the force component along the motion does work.

The cross product

a×b=​a2​b3​−a3​b2​a3​b1​−a1​b3​a1​b2​−a2​b1​​​,∣a×b∣=∣a∣∣b∣sinθ.

The result is perpendicular to both inputs, its direction follows the right-hand rule, and its length is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors span. Swapping the order flips the sign: b×a=−a×b.

The moment of a force F applied at position r about the origin is M=r×F. Its component along an axis u (a unit vector) is M⋅u, the twisting effect about that axis.

Worked exampleMoment on a bracket

A bracket bolted at the origin carries a cable force F=(30,−40,120) N attached at r=(0.2,0.5,0) m.

  1. Force magnitude: ∣F∣=302+402+1202​=130 N.
  2. Moment: M=r×F=(0.5⋅120−0⋅(−40),0⋅30−0.2⋅120,0.2⋅(−40)−0.5⋅30)=(60,−24,−23) N m.
  3. Size: ∣M∣=602+242+232​=68.6 N m.
  4. Twist about the bolt axis u=(0,0,1): Mz​=−23 N m, clockwise seen from above. That’s the torque the bolt must resist; the other two components bend it.
  5. Check: M⋅r=12−12+0=0 and M⋅F=1800+960−2760=0. The moment is perpendicular to both, as it must be.

Exercise 1Work along a ramp

A crate slides 4 m along a ramp in the direction s=4(0.8,0,−0.6) m while gravity F=(0,0,−490) N acts on it. Find the work done by gravity, and the component of gravity along the ramp.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Work: W=F⋅s=4(0+0+490⋅0.6)=1176 J.
  2. The ramp direction (0.8,0,−0.6) is already a unit vector, so the component along it is F⋅u=294 N.
  3. Check: 294 N×4 m=1176 J. The crate drops 4×0.6=2.4 m and 490×2.4=1176 J, the change in potential energy.

02.02.title: Systems of linear equations
02.02.html:
Equilibrium of a pin-jointed structure, currents in a circuit, a finite-element model with a million nodes: all of them end as Ax=b. Before solving big systems you need to see small ones two ways, as intersecting lines and as combinations of columns, and to know when a solution exists, is unique, and can be trusted.

Two pictures of the same equations

Take

2x−y−x+2y​=0=3​⟺(2−1​−12​)(xy​)=(03​).
  • Row picture: each equation is a line in the plane; the solution (1,2) is where they cross.
  • Column picture: find weights x,y so that x(2,−1)+y(−1,2)=(0,3). The solution says how much of each column builds the right-hand side.

The column picture scales to any size and is the one linear algebra is built on: Ax=b has a solution exactly when b is a combination of the columns of A.

Exist, unique, or neither

For a square n×n system there are three cases:

  1. One solution: the columns are independent (detA=0).
  2. No solution: the columns are dependent and b isn’t in their span (parallel lines).
  3. Infinitely many: dependent columns and b is in the span (the same line twice).

In a structure, case 2 or 3 means a mechanism: the bars can’t carry the load, or they can carry it in endless ways because something can move freely.

Nearly singular is the practical danger

Real data carries errors. If the two lines cross at a shallow angle, a tiny shift in one of them moves the crossing a long way. The condition number κ(A)=∥A∥∥A−1∥ measures this amplification: relative errors in b can grow by a factor up to κ in x.

Worked exampleForces in a two-bar joint

A joint carries a 10 kN load downward. Bar 1 leaves the joint at 150∘ from the x axis, bar 2 at 45∘. Call the bar forces T1​, T2​ (positive in tension, pulling the joint along the bar).

  1. Equilibrium in x: T1​cos150∘+T2​cos45∘=0.
  2. Equilibrium in y: T1​sin150∘+T2​sin45∘−10=0.
  3. Matrix form: (−0.86600.5​0.70710.7071​)(T1​T2​​)=(010​), with det=−0.966.
  4. Subtract the rows: −1.366T1​=−10, so T1​=7.32 kN, then T2​=0.866⋅7.32/0.7071=8.97 kN.

Both bars are in tension, and both carry less than 10 kN each only because they share the load at a good angle. Swing bar 2 towards 150∘ and the determinant goes to zero while the forces blow up.

Exercise 1A three-way check

For (12​24​)x=b, say whether there are zero, one or infinitely many solutions when b=(3,6) and when b=(3,5), and give the solutions where they exist.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The second column is twice the first, so detA=4−4=0 and the columns span only the line through (1,2).
  2. b=(3,6)=3(1,2) lies on that line: infinitely many solutions, x1​+2x2​=3, for example (3,0) or (1,1).
  3. b=(3,5) isn’t a multiple of (1,2): no solution. In the row picture the lines x1​+2x2​=3 and x1​+2x2​=2.5 are parallel.

02.03.title: Gaussian elimination
02.03.html:
Gaussian elimination is the algorithm behind every direct solver: subtract multiples of rows until the matrix is upper triangular, then solve from the bottom up. It’s short to write, and its two weak spots, small pivots and n3 cost, explain most of what professional solvers do differently.

Forward elimination

For column k, use the pivot akk​ to clear every entry below it. Row i becomes

rowi​←rowi​−ℓik​rowk​,ℓik​=akk​aik​​.

Apply the same operation to b. After n−1 columns the system is Ux=c with U upper triangular.

Back substitution

Solve the last equation first and work upwards:

xi​=uii​1​(ci​−j>i∑​uij​xj​).

Pivoting

If a pivot is zero the method stops; if it’s tiny the multipliers are huge and rounding errors swamp the answer. Partial pivoting swaps rows so the largest entry (in absolute value) in the column becomes the pivot. Consider

(10−201​11​)x=(12​),x≈(1,1).

Without a swap, ℓ=1020, the second row becomes (0,1−1020), and in double precision the 1 is lost. Back substitution gives x2​=1 and then x1​=0, completely wrong. With the swap the multiplier is 10−20 and the answer is right to machine precision.

Cost

Clearing column k touches an (n−k)×(n−k) block, so the total is about ∑k2⋅2≈32​n3 floating-point operations. Back substitution is only n2. Doubling the number of unknowns makes a dense solve eight times slower, which is why lesson 02.14 is about exploiting zeros.

Worked exampleElimination by hand

Solve ​2−3−2​1−11​−122​​x=​8−11−3​​ without pivoting, to see the mechanics.

  1. Column 1, pivot 2: ℓ21​=−1.5, ℓ31​=−1. Row 2 becomes (0, 0.5, 0.5∣1), row 3 becomes (0, 2, 1∣5).
  2. Column 2, pivot 0.5: ℓ32​=4. Row 3 becomes (0, 0, −1∣1).
  3. Back substitution: x3​=−1; 0.5x2​+0.5(−1)=1 gives x2​=3; 2x1​+3+1=8 gives x1​=2.
  4. Check row 2 of the original: −6−3−2=−11. Correct.

With partial pivoting, the first step would swap in row 2 (largest entry ∣−3∣). The answer is the same; the multipliers stay at most 1 in size.

Exercise 1Count the work

Estimate the floating-point operations for Gaussian elimination on a dense 10000×10000 system, and the time at 1011 operations per second (a good laptop with an optimised library). How does that compare with a 1000×1000 system?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 32​n3=32​×1012≈6.7×1011 operations.
  2. At 1011 per second: about 6.7 s.
  3. For n=1000: 6.7×108 operations, about 7 ms. Ten times the unknowns costs a thousand times the work.
  4. Memory matters too: 108 entries at 8 bytes is 800 MB just to store the matrix.

quiz.q: Why does partial pivoting pick the largest entry in the column?
quiz.explain: Small pivots give large multipliers that amplify rounding errors.
options: It makes the matrix symmetric
It keeps the multipliers at most 1 in size, limiting error growth
It reduces the operation count
It’s needed only for singular matrices

quiz.q: In the worked example, what is the multiplier ℓ32​ used in the second column?
quiz.explain: After step 1 the entries are 2 (row 3) and 0.5 (pivot).

quiz.q: Approximate floating-point operations (32​n3) for a dense solve with n=3000. Scientific notation is fine, for example 4.5e9.
quiz.explain: 32​×2.7×1010.

quiz.q: Without pivoting, the system with pivot 10−20 returns x1​=0. Why?
quiz.explain: Double precision keeps about 16 digits, so 1−1020 rounds to −1020.
options: The matrix is singular
The 1 in 1−1020 is lost to rounding, and back substitution then cancels badly
Python integers overflow
The right-hand side is wrong

02.04.title: LU decomposition
02.04.html:
A structure is analysed for many load cases: self-weight, wind from four directions, a crane at six positions. The stiffness matrix stays the same; only the right-hand side changes. LU decomposition stores the result of elimination once, so each new load case costs n2 operations instead of n3.

Elimination is a factorisation

The multipliers ℓik​ from Gaussian elimination aren’t thrown away. Put them below the diagonal of a unit lower-triangular matrix L, keep the eliminated matrix as U, and

A=LU.

With row swaps from pivoting, recorded in a permutation matrix P, the general form is PA=LU.

Solving with the factors

Ax=b becomes L(Ux)=b. Solve two triangular systems:

  1. Forward substitution: Ly=Pb, top to bottom.
  2. Back substitution: Ux=y, bottom to top.

Each costs about n2 operations. Factor once at 32​n3, then solve as many right-hand sides as you like.

Never form the inverse

A−1b is fine on paper. In code, computing A−1 costs about three times as much as LU, uses more memory for sparse matrices, and is less accurate. Keep the factors and solve.

Determinant for free

detL=1 and detU is the product of the pivots, so detA=±∏uii​, with the sign set by the number of row swaps. Lesson 02.05 uses this.

Worked exampleFactor once, solve twice

Take the matrix from lesson 02.03, A=​2−3−2​1−11​−122​​. The multipliers were ℓ21​=−1.5, ℓ31​=−1, ℓ32​=4, so

L=​1−1.5−1​014​001​​,U=​200​10.50​−10.5−1​​.

New load case b=(1,0,0):

  1. Forward: y1​=1; y2​=0+1.5⋅1=1.5; y3​=0+1−4⋅1.5=−5.
  2. Back: x3​=−5/(−1)=5; 0.5x2​+0.5⋅5=1.5 gives x2​=−2; 2x1​−2−5=1 gives x1​=4.
  3. Check: Ax=(8−2−5, −12+2+10, −8−2+10)=(1,0,0).

And detA=2×0.5×(−1)=−1, with no swaps.

Exercise 1When does LU pay off?

For n=2000, compare the operation count of solving 50 load cases by (a) repeating Gaussian elimination each time and (b) one LU factorisation plus 50 pairs of triangular solves.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. (a) 50×32​n3=50×5.33×109=2.67×1011.
  2. (b) 32​n3+50×2n2=5.33×109+4×108=5.73×109.
  3. LU is about 46 times cheaper. With one load case the two are the same; the gain grows with every extra right-hand side.

quiz.explain: Unit diagonal, multipliers below it.

quiz.explain: y3​=0−(−1)(1)−4(1.5).

02.05.title: Determinants and invertibility
02.05.html:
The determinant is one number that says whether a square system has a unique solution. Geometrically it’s the factor by which the matrix scales areas (in 2D) or volumes (in 3D). In a structure, a zero determinant of the stiffness matrix means something can move without resistance: a mechanism.

Area scaling

The 2×2 matrix A=(ac​bd​) maps the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by its columns (a,c) and (b,d). That parallelogram’s signed area is

detA=ad−bc,

the z component of the cross product of the columns from lesson 02.01. A negative value means the map flips orientation, like a mirror.

Rules that matter

  • det(AB)=detAdetB: scaling factors multiply.
  • detAT=detA.
  • Swapping two rows flips the sign; adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing.
  • det(cA)=cndetA for an n×n matrix.
  • detA=0 exactly when A is invertible, and then detA−1=1/detA.

How to compute it

Cofactor expansion is the textbook formula, but it costs about n! operations: for n=20 that’s 2.4×1018. Use elimination instead. Row operations of the “add a multiple” kind don’t change the determinant, so after elimination

detA=(−1)si∏​uii​,

where s counts the row swaps. That’s 32​n3 operations, the same as LU.

Small determinant doesn’t mean nearly singular

det(10−3I10​)=10−30, but that matrix is perfectly conditioned. Scale changes the determinant without changing how hard the system is. Use the condition number (lesson 02.12) to judge near-singularity.

Worked exampleA spring chain with and without its anchor

Three masses in a row, joined by springs of stiffness k, with the first one also tied to a wall. The stiffness matrix is

K=k​2−10​−12−1​0−11​​.
  1. Eliminate: pivots 2, then 2−21​=1.5, then 1−1.51​=31​.
  2. detK=k3⋅2⋅1.5⋅31​=k3. Nonzero, so every load gives a unique displacement.
  3. Now cut the wall spring. The first diagonal entry drops to 1: pivots 1, 1, 0. The determinant is zero.
  4. Physical reading: with no anchor, the vector (1,1,1), all masses shifted equally, stretches no spring. K(1,1,1)T=0, a rigid-body motion. Any solver will fail on that matrix, as it should.

Exercise 1Is the bracket a mechanism?

Two springs, k1​=400 N/mm and k2​=600 N/mm, connect a wall to node 1 and node 1 to node 2. Write the 2×2 stiffness matrix for the node displacements, compute its determinant, then repeat with k1​=0.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. K=(k1​+k2​−k2​​−k2​k2​​)=(1000−600​−600600​) N/mm.
  2. detK=1000⋅600−6002=240000 (N/mm)2, which equals k1​k2​. Invertible.
  3. With k1​=0: det=600⋅600−6002=0. Nothing holds the pair to the wall, so (1,1) is a free motion.

quiz.explain: ad−bc=12−2.

quiz.explain: det(cA)=cndetA=8×2.

The material is linear

quiz.explain: Product of pivots is 1; one swap flips the sign.

02.06.title: Vector spaces and rank
02.06.html:
Rank answers a practical question: how many independent equations do you actually have? A truss with a redundant bar, a sensor array with two sensors measuring the same thing, a free-floating part with rigid-body motions: each shows up as a rank deficiency. This lesson gives you the four ideas you need (span, independence, rank, null space) and the code to compute them reliably.

Span, independence, basis

The span of vectors v1​,…,vk​ is every combination c1​v1​+⋯+ck​vk​. The vectors are independent if the only combination giving 0 is all ci​=0. An independent spanning set is a basis, and every basis of a space has the same number of vectors: its dimension.

The column space and the null space

For an m×n matrix A:

  • The column space C(A) is the span of the columns: every Ax. Its dimension is the rank r.
  • The null space N(A) is every x with Ax=0.

They’re tied by the rank-nullity theorem:

rankA+dimN(A)=n(the number of columns).

So each independent way the system can move freely costs one rank.

Computing rank in floating point

In exact arithmetic, rank is the number of nonzero pivots. In floating point, a “zero” pivot comes out as 10−17, so you need a tolerance. The robust tool is the singular value decomposition (lesson 02.12): rank is the number of singular values above εσmax​max(m,n). The code below implements reduced row echelon form with a tolerance and compares it with the SVD answer.

Worked exampleCount the free motions

The free three-mass chain from lesson 02.05 has

K=​1−10​−12−1​0−11​​.
  1. Row reduce: add row 1 to row 2 to get (0,1,−1); add the new row 2 to row 3 to get (0,0,0).
  2. Two nonzero pivots, so rankK=2.
  3. Rank-nullity: dimN(K)=3−2=1.
  4. The null space: from row 2, x2​=x3​; from row 1, x1​=x2​. So N(K) is spanned by (1,1,1), the rigid shift.
  5. Fix one node (delete its row and column) and the rank of the remaining 2×2 matrix is 2: the system is solvable.

Exercise 1Supports for a triangle

The free triangle truss has three rigid-body motions. You pin node 1 (fixing u1​ and v1​). What’s the rank of the remaining 4×4 stiffness matrix, and is it enough? Where would you put one more support, and in which direction?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Pinning removes the two translations but not the rotation about node 1, so the remaining 4×4 matrix has rank 3 and one null vector.
  2. Not enough: the triangle can still spin about the pin.
  3. Add a roller at node 2 that stops motion perpendicular to the line from node 1 to node 2: for nodes (0,0) and (2,0), fix v2​. Now the matrix that’s left is 3×3 with rank 3.
  4. A roller at node 2 fixing u2​ would fail, because rotating about node 1 moves node 2 vertically, not horizontally.

02.07.title: Orthogonality and least squares
02.07.html:
You measure a spring at six extensions and get six forces. Hooke’s law has two unknowns (stiffness and an offset), so six equations can’t all hold exactly: the data is noisy. Least squares picks the line that makes the total squared error smallest, and the reason it works is pure geometry: the best fit is an orthogonal projection.

Overdetermined systems

With more equations than unknowns, Ax=b usually has no solution because b isn’t in the column space of A. Instead, minimise the length of the residual r=b−Ax:

xmin​∥b−Ax∥22​.

The projection picture

Ax ranges over the column space. The closest point to b in that space is its orthogonal projection, so at the optimum the residual is perpendicular to every column:

AT(b−Ax^)=0⟹ATAx^=ATb.

These are the normal equations. If the columns of A are independent, ATA is invertible and the fit is unique.

Don’t solve the normal equations blindly

ATA squares the condition number: if κ(A)=106, then κ(ATA)=1012 and you’ve lost twelve of your sixteen digits. For small, well-scaled fits like the one below the normal equations are fine. For anything else, use QR (lesson 02.08) or the SVD, which is what np.linalg.lstsq does.

Worked exampleFitting a spring test

Extensions x=0,1,2,3,4,5 mm, forces F=0.1,2.6,4.7,7.4,9.6,12.1 N. Model F=kx+F0​.

  1. A has columns x and 1. Then ATA=(∑x2∑x​∑x6​)=(5515​156​) and ATF=(∑xF∑F​)=(133.136.5​).
  2. Determinant 55⋅6−152=105.
  3. k=(6⋅133.1−15⋅36.5)/105=251.1/105=2.391 N/mm.
  4. F0​=(55⋅36.5−15⋅133.1)/105=11/105=0.105 N.
  5. Residual norm ∥r∥=0.259 N, and ATr=0 to rounding: the residual is orthogonal to both columns.

Forcing the line through the origin (F0​=0) gives k=∑xF/∑x2=133.1/55=2.420 N/mm. Whether to include the offset is a modelling decision: a real load cell usually has one.

Exercise 1Average as least squares

You measure one length four times: 12.02, 11.98, 12.05, 11.99 mm. Write this as an overdetermined system Ax=b for the single unknown L, solve the normal equations, and say what you’ve found.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=(1,1,1,1)T, b=(12.02,11.98,12.05,11.99)T.
  2. ATA=4 and ATb=48.04, so L^=12.01 mm.
  3. That’s the arithmetic mean. Least squares with one constant unknown always gives the average, and the residuals (0.01,−0.03,0.04,−0.02) sum to zero: orthogonal to (1,1,1,1).

02.08.title: QR and Gram-Schmidt
02.08.html:
Orthonormal bases make everything easy: coordinates are dot products, projections are sums, and nothing amplifies rounding error. The QR decomposition turns any set of independent columns into an orthonormal set Q plus an upper-triangular record R of how to rebuild the originals. It’s the standard way to do least squares, and the first step of the QR eigenvalue algorithm.

Gram-Schmidt

Process the columns a1​,a2​,… in order. Subtract from each the parts along the directions you already have, then normalise:

vj​=aj​−i<j∑​(qi​⋅aj​)qi​,qj​=∥vj​∥vj​​.

The coefficients are the entries of R: rij​=qi​⋅aj​ and rjj​=∥vj​∥. Then A=QR, with QTQ=I.

Classical versus modified

The formula above (classical Gram-Schmidt) computes every rij​ from the original aj​. If the columns are nearly dependent, the q's it produces drift away from orthogonal. Modified Gram-Schmidt subtracts one direction at a time from the running vector, which is the same in exact arithmetic but much better in floating point. Householder reflections, used by LAPACK and np.linalg.qr, are better still: Q is orthogonal to machine precision regardless of conditioning.

Exercise 1Orthonormalise three vectors

Apply Gram-Schmidt to a1​=(1,0,0), a2​=(1,1,0), a3​=(1,1,1). What are Q and R?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. q1​=(1,0,0), r11​=1.
  2. r12​=q1​⋅a2​=1; v2​=(0,1,0), so r22​=1 and q2​=(0,1,0).
  3. r13​=1, r23​=1; v3​=(0,0,1), r33​=1.
  4. Q=I and R=​100​110​111​​, which is A itself: A was already upper triangular.
